_provenance.severity_model: Since flag-001, severity derives from risk, not consensus. A rule blocks only if `unambiguous` (the regex means one thing) AND `rarely_legitimate` (almost nobody wants this on purpose) are both true. Every warn rule carries `risk_note` saying which test it failed.
_provenance.why_changed: Catalog count measures how contested a pattern is. It says nothing about whether refusing on it will ever be wrong. design-005 conflated the two; flag-001 separates them.
_provenance.catalogs_field: Retained as provenance only. Counts are reconstructed from published descriptions and write-ups, NOT verified against source rule files. Severity no longer depends on them, which lowers the cost of that gap, but they are still unverified.
_provenance.authored_by: The `rarely_legitimate` calls are judgments, not measurements. They are the thing to audit if a block ever fires on legitimate code.

not_shipped.wcag-contrast: True contrast ratio needs computed style. The lexical proxy ships as `default-grey-body`.
not_shipped.centered-text-density: A whole-page measurement, not a write-time match.
not_shipped.dead-hover-states: Requires knowing what the hover does.

_provenance.corpus_validation: Validated against shadcn/ui, tailwindcss.com and cal.com. The first run refused 32.7% of tailwindcss.com, which exposed three wrong `rarely_legitimate` calls (dark-mode grey text, backdrop-blur on navs, John Doe as an input placeholder) and four rules that had to be demoted. Demonstration directories are exempt from the copy and asset rules only , placeholder content is correct in a demo; a purple gradient is not. Second pass: default-grey-body demoted (grey on dark is correct and undetectable by regex), and test/fixture directories exempted from every rule.
_provenance.method: Patterns are drawn from publicly documented catalogs of AI design tells: impeccable (https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable), Taste Skill (https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill), Anthropic's frontend-design skill (https://github.com/anthropics/skills/tree/main/skills/frontend-design), the UI/UX Pro Max anti-pattern database, and several independent 2026 write-ups.
_provenance.correction: An earlier version of this file cited a catalog called 'web-taste'. That could not be verified as a distinct project and has been removed. Some `catalogs` counts may therefore be overstated by one. Since flag-001 those counts are provenance only and do not affect severity.

rules.because: The purple-to-violet gradient is the single strongest tell of machine-made UI. Models reach for it because it sits under thousands of SaaS landing pages in the training data.
rules.instead: One flat colour chosen for this project. If you want depth, use spacing and type weight, not a gradient.
rules.catches: Purple, violet or indigo gradient stops

rules.because: These are the exact hex values models default to for 'primary'. Seeing one hardcoded means the colour was inherited, not chosen.
rules.instead: Define your own value. Any deliberate hue beats the one that arrived by default.
rules.catches: The seven hex values models pick for 'primary'

rules.because: A three-stop gradient is decoration with no informational job. It is the 'make it look exciting' reflex.
rules.instead: One colour, or a two-stop gradient with a reason. Excitement comes from contrast, not from hue count.
rules.catches: Gradients with three or more colour stops

rules.because: Tailwind's mid-blue as the primary brand colour is the framework default wearing a brand's clothes.
rules.instead: Define one project colour and use it. Any deliberate hue beats the palette you got for free.
rules.risk_note: Plenty of real products deliberately use a mid-blue, and Tailwind's is a reasonable one.
rules.catches: bg-blue-500 or bg-blue-600 as the brand colour

rules.because: Light grey body text is the most common accessibility failure in generated UI, and it reads as washed out rather than subtle. Dark-mode variants are excluded, since dark:text-gray-400 is correct.
rules.instead: Body copy at full strength. If something should recede, reduce its size or weight, not its contrast.
rules.risk_note: Correct on dark surfaces. tailwindcss.com pairs text-gray-400 with text-white, and a regex cannot see the background colour, so this advises.
rules.catches: Light grey body text on a light background

rules.because: A coloured shadow is a glow with extra steps. It is the most-copied way to make a button look special without deciding anything.
rules.instead: Neutral shadow, or none. If the element needs to stand out, change its size, weight or position.
rules.catches: Coloured shadows like shadow-purple-500/50

rules.because: A gradient across the whole page background is the default 'premium' move and it fights every piece of content placed on it.
rules.instead: A flat background. Let the content carry the interest.
rules.catches: A gradient applied to the page background itself

rules.risk_note: Legitimate in high-contrast and print-like designs, so it advises rather than refuses.
rules.because: Pure black on pure white is harsher than print ever was and reads as untuned.
rules.instead: Near-black around #14141a. The eye reads it as black and it stops vibrating.
rules.catches: Pure #000 text

rules.risk_note: One-off arbitrary colours are sometimes correct, so this advises.
rules.because: Arbitrary hex values scattered through markup means there is no palette. Every colour was decided separately and none of them relate.
rules.instead: Put the value in your theme and use the token. If it is worth using twice it is worth naming.
rules.catches: Arbitrary hex values inline in class names

rules.because: Inter is the default of defaults. It is not a bad typeface; it is the one chosen when nobody chose.
rules.instead: Pick a face with a point of view and commit to it. Name it in the project's own styles.
rules.catches: Inter declared as the typeface

rules.risk_note: The system stack is a legitimate choice for utilities and docs, so this advises.
rules.because: The system stack alone is the absence of a typographic decision. It is fine for a tool and wrong for anything with a voice.
rules.instead: Choose a face for headings at least. One deliberate typeface changes the whole impression.
rules.catches: The system font stack as the only typographic choice

rules.risk_note: Counting occurrences in a window is a proxy, and a dense component can trip it legitimately.
rules.because: When everything is bold nothing is. Uniform heavy weight is what happens when hierarchy was never decided.
rules.instead: One or two weights doing different jobs. Let size and space carry the rest.
rules.catches: font-bold repeated until nothing stands out

rules.risk_note: Genuinely correct in editorial layouts, so it advises rather than refuses.
rules.because: The tiny uppercase letterspaced kicker above every heading is a template convention, repeated until it means nothing.
rules.instead: Say it in the heading, or drop it. A label that adds no information is decoration.
rules.catches: The tiny uppercase letterspaced kicker above a heading

rules.risk_note: Deliberate editorial and display work uses these sizes properly.
rules.because: Enormous hero type is how generated pages signal importance without earning it. At this size the words usually say less than the space they take.
rules.instead: Drop a step or two and give the line something worth reading.
rules.catches: text-7xl and above

rules.because: A zero-offset glow is decoration standing in for hierarchy. Neon-on-dark with glowing borders is the v0 and Cursor signature.
rules.instead: Offset shadows describe light and depth. If the element needs emphasis, give it size, weight or space.
rules.catches: Zero-offset box shadows used as a glow

rules.because: The default heavy drop shadow on every card is how generated UI signals 'this is a component'. Real interfaces use shadow sparingly and at one or two depths.
rules.instead: A hairline border, or a shadow one or two steps lighter. Reserve the heaviest depth for things that actually float.
rules.risk_note: shadow-xl is the right depth for modals, popovers and dropdowns that genuinely float.
rules.catches: shadow-xl and shadow-2xl on ordinary cards

rules.because: Frosted glass on everything is the current default for 'make it look premium'. Applied without a reason it flattens hierarchy and wrecks contrast.
rules.instead: Solid surfaces. If you want separation, use a different background value or real spacing.
rules.risk_note: Correct for translucent navs, modal scrims and overlays. Observed on sticky headers in cal.com; blocking it would break standard practice.
rules.catches: Frosted glass via backdrop-blur

rules.because: The giant blurred colour blob floating behind the hero is pure decoration, and it is in every generated landing page written since 2023.
rules.instead: Delete it. If the background needs interest, use a real edge, a rule, or a change of surface.
rules.catches: The blurred colour blob floating behind a hero

rules.because: Oversized rounding on every surface is a named tell. When cards, buttons and inputs share one bubbly radius, nothing reads as a different kind of thing.
rules.instead: Pick one radius for the project and vary it deliberately: tighter on inputs, looser on containers.
rules.risk_note: rounded-3xl is a legitimate deliberate choice for soft design systems.
rules.catches: rounded-3xl applied to every surface

rules.because: The one-pixel gradient wrapper faking a glowing border is a copied trick, not a design decision.
rules.instead: A real border in one colour. If the edge needs emphasis, change the surface inside it.
rules.catches: A 1px gradient wrapper faking a glowing border

rules.because: A four-digit z-index means the stacking order was never designed, only fought with.
rules.instead: Fix the stacking context. If two things overlap, one of them is in the wrong place in the tree.
rules.catches: Four-digit z-index values

rules.risk_note: Rings have legitimate decorative uses, and the focus-state exclusion here is a rough proxy.
rules.because: Rings used as decoration rather than focus states dilute the one signal keyboard users depend on.
rules.instead: Keep ring for focus. For emphasis use a border or a background change.
rules.catches: Focus rings used as ornament

rules.risk_note: Some design systems legitimately use both together.
rules.because: A border and a shadow on the same element is two solutions to one problem, applied because neither was chosen.
rules.instead: Pick one. Borders suit dense interfaces, shadows suit floating things.
rules.catches: A border and a shadow doing the same job

rules.match: >\s*(?:Get Started|Get started|Learn More|Learn more|Click Here|Sign Up Free|Try It Free|Try for free|Read More)\s*<
rules.because: A call to action that says nothing about what happens next is the same button on ten thousand pages.
rules.instead: Name the action in the user's words. 'Start a 14-day trial', 'See it running', 'Read the first chapter'.
rules.catches: Buttons that say Get Started, Learn More, Click Here

rules.match: <h[12][^>]*>\s*(?:Welcome(?: to)?\b|Everything you need\b|The future of\b|Supercharge your\b|Build the future\b|Unlock the power\b|Transform your\b|Elevate your\b|Take your \w+ to the next level\b)
rules.because: A headline that could sit on any product's page tells the reader nothing and wastes the only line they are guaranteed to read.
rules.instead: Say what this specific thing does for this specific person, in their words.
rules.catches: Headlines like Transform your workflow or Unlock the power

rules.because: Marketing vocabulary with no referent. These words survive because they are hard to disagree with, which is exactly why they persuade nobody.
rules.instead: Replace the adjective with the fact underneath it. 'Seamless' usually means 'no configuration'. Say that.
rules.catches: Seamless, cutting-edge, revolutionary, game-changing

rules.because: Placeholder copy in a real component means the content question was skipped, and skipped content is where generic layouts come from.
rules.instead: Write the actual sentence, even badly. Real copy changes the layout you need.
rules.catches: Placeholder latin left in a real component

rules.because: Template scaffolding that shipped. It signals that nobody read the page after it was generated.
rules.instead: Write the real thing, or delete the element until you have it.
rules.catches: Your Company, Text goes here, Replace this

rules.because: Invented social proof is worse than none. Placeholder names rendered as testimonial text are the clearest sign the section was generated wholesale.
rules.instead: Real quotes with real names, or remove the section until you have them.
rules.catches: John Doe or Acme Inc rendered as social proof

rules.match: //\s*(?:In a real (?:implementation|app|world)|This is a simplified|For demonstration purposes|Note: [Tt]his is a placeholder|Mock data for now)|as an AI\b
rules.because: A comment apologising for the code being a sketch. It is the most direct evidence possible that generated output shipped unread.
rules.instead: Either finish it or delete the branch. A comment is not a substitute for a decision.
rules.catches: Comments like // In a real implementation this would

rules.risk_note: Genuine exclamations exist and this cannot tell them apart.
rules.because: Exclamation marks in interface copy are enthusiasm applied to a reader who did not ask for it.
rules.instead: Say it flat. If the news is good the reader will supply the feeling.
rules.catches: Exclamation marks in interface copy

rules.risk_note: Entirely legitimate once the logos are real.
rules.because: The logo strip is a template slot. When it appears before there are real customers, it is a slot filled rather than a claim made.
rules.instead: Only if the logos are real and you have permission. Otherwise the space is better empty.
rules.catches: A Trusted by logo strip

rules.risk_note: Correct and necessary for products where the AI is the point.
rules.because: Saying it is AI-powered describes the implementation, not the benefit. It is the first thing generated copy reaches for.
rules.instead: Say what it does for the reader. They do not care what is behind it.
rules.catches: Copy that sells the implementation rather than the benefit

rules.because: Hot-linked stock photography is a placeholder that ships. It breaks offline, leaks referrers, and guarantees someone else's site looks identical.
rules.instead: A real asset in the repo, or an honest empty state. A blank space beats a stranger's photograph.
rules.catches: Hot-linked Unsplash, placehold.co or picsum URLs

rules.because: Procedurally generated avatars are the visual equivalent of Lorem ipsum, and they make every user look like a placeholder.
rules.instead: Initials on a flat background, or the user's real image. Both beat a robot face.
rules.catches: Procedural avatars from dicebear or ui-avatars

rules.because: Emoji standing in for an icon system is a named tell. It renders differently on every platform and signals that no icon decision was made.
rules.instead: A real icon set, or no icon. If the label needs an emoji to carry meaning, the label needs rewriting.
rules.catches: Emoji standing in for an icon inside headings or buttons

rules.risk_note: A legitimate choice for genuinely magical actions, so it advises.
rules.because: The sparkle icon is the universal shorthand for 'this bit is AI'. It arrived with the first wave of AI products and has meant nothing since.
rules.instead: An icon that describes the action. If the action is 'generate', draw generating.
rules.catches: The sparkle or wand icon as shorthand for AI

rules.risk_note: Named by four catalogs, but grid-cols-3 fires constantly on legitimate tables and galleries.
rules.because: Three equal-weight cards in a row is the default answer to 'show some features', repeated for every section. It gives every item the same importance, which usually means none were ranked.
rules.instead: Decide which one matters most and let the layout say so.
rules.catches: Three equal cards as a page's main content

rules.risk_note: A perfectly reasonable width that many real projects pick deliberately.
rules.because: Every generated page is 1280px centred. It is not wrong, it is the width nobody chose, and it makes unrelated products feel like the same site.
rules.instead: Pick a measure from your type. Long-form reading wants far narrower; a dashboard usually wants wider.
rules.catches: max-w-7xl mx-auto, the width nobody chose

rules.risk_note: Centred sections are correct for short hero content.
rules.because: Centred everything is the layout equivalent of a shrug. Centred text is hard to read in paragraphs and removes the left edge the eye scans against.
rules.instead: Left-align body copy. Centre only short, deliberate lines.
rules.catches: Whole sections centre-aligned

rules.risk_note: Requires structural nesting analysis; this regex is a shallow proxy that will miss most real cases.
rules.because: Everything wrapped in a card, then cards inside cards. Three levels of container, because hierarchy was never decided.
rules.instead: One container. Use spacing to group what is inside it.
rules.catches: A card inside a card

rules.risk_note: Needs relative sizing and position to detect properly; also fires on large avatars.
rules.because: The big circled icon floating above a centred heading is a named tell. The decoration is sized larger than the message it introduces.
rules.instead: Lose the circle. If the icon earns its place, let it sit inline at text scale.
rules.catches: A large circled icon floating above a heading

rules.risk_note: Legitimate for genuine full-screen experiences.
rules.because: A hero that fills the viewport before saying anything is the template default. It costs the reader a scroll to learn nothing.
rules.instead: Size the section to its content. Let the next thing peek above the fold.
rules.catches: min-h-screen on the first thing a reader sees

rules.risk_note: Counting in a window is a proxy and can trip on legitimate layouts.
rules.because: More than one sticky element and the viewport belongs to the chrome rather than the content.
rules.instead: One sticky thing at most. Everything else can scroll away.
rules.catches: More than one sticky element competing for the viewport

rules.risk_note: Detection requires counting chips per view; one Badge is fine, nine is the problem.
rules.because: Badges everywhere is what happens when nothing was prioritised. Every state gets a chip and none of them read.
rules.instead: Keep the one or two states a user acts on. Put the rest in text.
rules.catches: Four or more badges in one view

rules.risk_note: p-0 and p-1 are correct constantly in dense and nested layouts.
rules.because: Interfaces generated without a spacing decision default to too tight. Padding is the cheapest quality signal there is.
rules.instead: Start generous and remove. If it looks empty, the type is probably too small.
rules.catches: p-0 and p-1 where breathing room was needed

rules.risk_note: One-off values are sometimes exactly right.
rules.because: Arbitrary pixel values mean there is no spacing scale. Every gap was decided in isolation.
rules.instead: Use the scale. If nothing on the scale fits, the scale is wrong and should change.
rules.catches: Arbitrary pixel spacing off the scale

rules.risk_note: Small buttons inside dense toolbars are a legitimate pattern.
rules.because: A button under about 44px is hard to hit and reads as an afterthought.
rules.instead: Give interactive targets room. Pad the hit area even when the icon stays small.
rules.catches: Buttons under roughly 44px

rules.risk_note: A single deliberate entrance animation is fine; this cannot tell one from forty.
rules.because: The same fade-in on every element is motion applied as a finish rather than to show a relationship. It delays everything and explains nothing.
rules.instead: Animate what changes meaning: a thing arriving, a state flipping. Leave the rest still.
rules.catches: The same entrance animation on everything

rules.risk_note: Correct for genuinely playful products and for attention-seeking affordances like scroll cues.
rules.because: Overshoot easing on interface motion reads as playful once and cheap thereafter.
rules.instead: Ease-out for things entering, ease-in for things leaving. No overshoot on anything a user waits for.
rules.catches: Overshoot easing on interface motion

rules.risk_note: Entirely correct for loading skeletons, which is where most matches will be.
rules.because: A pulsing element that is not loading anything is an animation looking for a job.
rules.instead: Keep pulse for skeletons and live indicators. Everything else can hold still.
rules.catches: animate-pulse on something that is not loading

rules.risk_note: Long durations are right for deliberate, large movements.
rules.because: Transitions over about half a second stop reading as responsive and start reading as lag.
rules.instead: 150ms to 300ms for most interface motion. Reserve longer for things genuinely travelling a distance.
rules.catches: Transitions over half a second

rules.risk_note: Whether dark is a reflex or a decision cannot be read from a class name.
rules.because: Dark by default is the most common reflex in generated interfaces. Dark is a real choice for some products and a costume for most.
rules.instead: Decide. If the product is used in daylight by people reading text, light is probably right.
rules.catches: A near-black page background as the default

rules.risk_note: Genuinely dynamic values must be inline.
rules.because: Inline styles bypass whatever system exists, which means the value was chosen locally and relates to nothing.
rules.instead: Put it in the stylesheet or the theme. If it is truly dynamic, that is the exception, not the habit.
rules.catches: Values set inline, bypassing the system

rules.risk_note: Overriding third-party CSS sometimes leaves no alternative.
rules.because: An !important is a note saying the cascade was lost. It is usually a symptom of a system that was never designed.
rules.instead: Fix the specificity. If you are overriding a third-party style, scope it instead.
rules.catches: !important

rules.risk_note: The negative lookaheads are a crude proxy for 'has a label' and will misfire on wrapped components.
rules.because: A placeholder used as the only label disappears the moment someone types, and takes the field's meaning with it.
rules.instead: A real label above the field. Placeholders are for examples, not names.
rules.catches: A placeholder used as the only label
